summary:
A proverb is a short, compressed saying about how life usually goes. The book opens, "These are the proverbs of Solomon son of David, king of Israel" (1:1) — the king who "composed three thousand proverbs" according to 1 Kings 4:32 — but it is a set of collections, and it labels them itself: "The proverbs of Solomon" (10:1), the "thirty sayings" of the wise (22:17–20), more Solomon "copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah" (25:1) two centuries later — the book documents its own editing — "the words of Agur son of Jakeh" (30:1), and the words of King Lemuel, "the burden that his mother taught him" (31:1). Its motto brackets the opening chapters: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge" (1:7), "the beginning of wisdom" (9:10) — fear here meaning reverent awe. "Wisdom" is Hebrew hokhmah, the word Exodus 31:3 uses for the tabernacle craftsman's "skill."

Chapters 1–9 are a father's speeches to "my son," warning against violent gain, adultery, debt-pledges, and laziness, and pressing him to get wisdom. Wisdom is personified as a woman: "Wisdom calls out in the street, she lifts her voice in the square" (1:20). In chapter 8 she speaks from before creation — "The LORD created me as His first course, before His works of old" (8:22) — lines early Christian writers connected with Christ, "the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). Chapter 9 sets rival banquets: Wisdom builds her house and sets her table; Folly, "naive and knows nothing," offers stolen water; both call to passersby with the identical line, "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" (9:4, 16).

From 10:1 the book shifts to two-line sayings built on parallelism, Hebrew poetry's habit of pairing lines that echo or, most often here, contrast: "A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (15:1); "Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it" (22:6). As is often noted, a proverb is a generalization, not a guarantee — the book itself sets opposite advice back to back, "Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be like him" beside "Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become wise in his own eyes" (26:4–5) — which to follow depends on the moment.

Two collections close the book. Agur starts from ignorance — "Surely I am the most ignorant of men" (30:2) — and speaks mostly in numbered lists: "There are three things too wonderful for me, four that I cannot understand" (30:18). King Lemuel's mother warns her son off wine and charges him, "Open your mouth for those with no voice" (31:8). The final poem asks, "A wife of noble character, who can find?" (31:10), then portrays her buying a field, planting a vineyard, and trading in what she makes; its twenty-two verses form an acrostic, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The book ends: "Give her the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her at the gates" (31:31).
